entries.title: Knapping stone
entries.summary: Strike one stone with another on a hard anvil to shape a cutting blade, an axe head or a digging blade. Light taps sharpen; heavy blows reshape.

sections.text: Stone breaks in a predictable way: strike it near an edge and a flake shears off, leaving a scar. Every strike is a cut through the stone, and the shape you end up with is simply the cobble minus all those flakes. Where you strike, how hard, and on which face decide everything.

steps: Carry at least two stones: one to shape, one to strike with.
Hold one, aim at the top of a hard surface - the flat stone, the top of the outcrop or a boulder - and press [key]E[/key]. The mossy log and the ground are too soft.

Choose the form with [key]1[/key], [key]2[/key] or [key]3[/key] (or the [key]Wheel[/key]): cutting blade, axe head or digging blade. Its outline appears on the stone in chalk, with the working edge marked.
Aim at the stone's rim - a small marker shows where the hammerstone will land - and strike with [key]LMB[/key].
Press [key]Enter[/key] when it looks right. [key]Esc[/key] steps away and leaves the stone on the anvil; press [key]E[/key] on it later to carry on.

sections.text: A quick tap of [key]LMB[/key] presses off a small, shallow flake: it thins and sharpens the edge right there without changing the outline much. Hold the button to wind up and the blow grows heavier as a ring fills around the cursor; once it reads heavy blow, it takes off a deep flake and moves the outline. Each flake shapes only a short stretch of edge, so work your way around.
Each flake comes off the face that is up. A thin, sharp edge has to be worked from both sides, so turn the stone over often with [key]RMB[/key].

sections.caption: Cutting blade, axe head and digging blade: the outlines the chalk shows.
list: [b]Cutting blade[/b] ([key]1[/key]): a leaf-shaped flake. Only one of its long edges has to be thin and sharp. It is a tool the moment you finish it: it cuts grass and branches and carves wood.
[b]Axe head[/b] ([key]2[/key]): a wedge with a narrow butt and a wide, curved bit. The whole bit must be thinned from both faces. Haft it to make an axe.
[b]Digging blade[/b] ([key]3[/key]): broad and flat, with a wide working edge. Haft it to make a digging tool.

sections.text: Two gauges on the right show how you are doing. [b]Outline[/b] is how well the stone fills the chalk shape without much left over outside it. [b]Working edge[/b] is how thin the marked edge is, right at the rim and just behind it. The middle of the stone must also stay thick enough not to snap. The finished piece's quality - Crude, Rough, Decent, Good, Fine or Excellent - comes about half from the outline and a little less from the edge.

list: [b]Too much knocked away[/b]: the stone has shrunk inside the chalk line. Heavy blows near the outline take more than you'd think.
[b]Excess stone outside the line[/b]: knock it off with heavy blows.
[b]A thick, blunt edge[/b]: light taps along it, from both faces.
[b]Crack![/b] A heavy blow across a narrow part of the stone can snap it in two. Save heavy blows for where the stone is broad.
[b]Finishing too early[/b]: a stone that isn't usable yet comes back to you as a rough, shapeless piece. Wait until the tip under the gauges says it looks usable.

sections.tip: Plan the shape before the first strike: rough out the outline with a few heavy blows where the stone is broad, then switch to light taps along the edge and turn the stone over often.

entries.title: Cordage
entries.summary: Two bundles of plant fiber, twisted and plied under your palm, make about a meter of strong cord for hafting tools and lashing buildings.

sections.text: A loose bundle of fiber pulls apart easily. Twist two bundles hard and let them wind back around each other, and the twists lock together into two-ply cord: strong, flexible and about a meter long.

steps: Carry at least two bundles of plant fiber.
Hold one, aim at a flat surface - the flat stone, a boulder, the mossy log or just bare ground - and press [key]E[/key].
Hold [key]LMB[/key] and roll the mouse left and right in long, steady strokes, as if rolling fiber along your thigh.
Keep going. The Length gauge fills, and when it is full the cord is done and goes into your pack.

list: The Evenness gauge shows how regular your strokes are.
Step away with [key]Esc[/key] and the half-made cord waits where it is. Gather it up instead ([key]LMB[/key] on it) and you get your fiber back.
A few short fibers are lost in the twisting; they go back into the soil.

sections.text: Every hafted tool needs one cordage, and platforms, posts, railings, ladders, roofs, shelves and sleeping mats are all lashed with it. When a hafted tool finally wears out, its cord frays back into a single bundle of fiber.

sections.tip: Wild fiber grass grows back after harvesting, and every harvest gives a few seeds - enough to plant a whole fiber patch.

track.text: Carry two bundles of plant fiber

entries.title: Hafting tools
entries.summary: Bind a knapped axe head or digging blade to a stick with cordage to make a real tool. How well you seat and bind it decides how well it works and how long it lasts.

sections.text: A stone head on its own is just a sharp rock. Seated against the end of a straight stick and bound tight with cord, it becomes a lever: an axe that chops limbs and fells trees, or a digging tool that digs about three times as much as your hands and tills soil for planting.

steps: Knap an axe head or a digging blade. A cutting blade needs no handle.
Carry a stick and one cordage.
Hold the head, aim at a flat surface or bare ground and press [key]E[/key].
[b]Seat[/b]: drag the head with [key]LMB[/key] to the end of the handle; the [key]Wheel[/key] turns it. An axe's edge runs in line with the handle; a digging blade's runs across it.
[b]Bind[/b]: hold [key]LMB[/key] and circle the mouse around the joint to wind the cord on. Six to eleven turns hold well.
[b]Tighten[/b]: hold [key]RMB[/key] and drag down to pull it tight. Then press [key]Enter[/key].

sections.text: A tool's quality comes mostly from its head - how well it was knapped - then from how well it sits on the handle and how well it is bound. A loose binding, less than half tight, wears out sooner, and a crooked head works less well. Fewer than six turns or more than eleven make a weaker binding, and you can't finish with fewer than three.

Every cut, chop and scoop wears a tool a little; better tools and tighter bindings wear more slowly. Its description shows its quality and how worn it is, and a worn tool works more weakly. When it finally breaks, a blade is simply gone. An axe or digging tool gives back its stick, its dulled stone head and a bundle of fiber from the frayed cord.

list: [b]Cutting blade[/b]: cuts grass and the tree's small branches, cuts up branches, and carves a stick into a hearth board.
[b]Axe[/b]: everything a blade does except cutting grass, and more - chopping off limbs, felling the trunk, chopping up limbs and splitting logs.
[b]Digging tool[/b]: digs earth and clay, tills soil for planting, and turns compost quickly.

sections.warn: A dulled or failed stone head can't be hafted: only a proper axe head or digging blade fits a handle.
